evidence.quote: John Philip Holland Submarine design, 1870s–1900s Irish immigrant John Philip Holland designed and constructed the U.S. Navy’s first submarine, USS Holland (SS 1). John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at Holland ’s more successful design. Holland included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system. After two years of Navy trials and modifications to Holland, the Navy purchased the submarine on April 11, 1900, for $165,000 (about $4.7 million today). It also ordered seven more Holland -type boats, sufficiently impressed by Holland ’s potential. On October 12, 1900, the U.S. Navy commissioned USS Holland as its first submarine, establishing the U.S. Submarine Force. USS Holland spent most of her ten years in service at the U.S. Naval Academy as a training submarine. The seven new Holland- type submarines, built with Navy-specified improvements, became the Navy’s A -class of submarines.

Able to dive to and accurately maintain a significant depth [up of 75 feet (23 m)]. Diving planes provide the means to precisely control depth [stern planes only, located behind the propeller]. Dual propulsion systems driving a single propeller at the stern. evidence.quote: John Philip Holland Submarine design, 1870s–1900s Irish immigrant John Philip Holland designed and constructed the U.S. Navy’s first submarine, USS Holland (SS 1). John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at Holland ’s more successful design. Holland included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system. After two years of Navy trials and modifications to Holland, the Navy purchased the submarine on April 11, 1900, for $165,000 (about $4.7 million today). It also ordered seven more Holland -type boats, sufficiently impressed by Holland ’s potential. On October 12, 1900, the U.S. Navy commissioned USS Holland as its first submarine, establishing the U.S. Submarine Force. USS Holland spent most of her ten years in service at the U.S. Naval Academy as a training submarine. The seven new Holland- type submarines, built with Navy-specified improvements, became the Navy’s A -class of submarines.

research_payload.counter_arguments: Boundary dispute: Lafayette class vs. separate James Madison/Benjamin Franklin classes. Some sources list James Madison (SSBN-627 to 636) and Benjamin Franklin (SSBN-640 to 645) as distinct classes; NHHC and most authoritative sources treat as subgroups of Lafayette class with minor improvements. Decision: combined under Lafayette to avoid padding roster with near-identical variants per DvsU guidance. Boundary dispute: Ohio SSGN conversions. Four Ohio-class boats converted to cruise missile role 2002-2008; some sources list as separate SSGN class. Decision: noted within Ohio class entry as conversions, not separate class. Boundary dispute: Columbia class inclusion. Lead boat under construction (65% complete Feb 2026) but not commissioned as of 2026. Decision: excluded because 'Ever Built' title for submarines means commissioned submarines; delivery expected 2028, first patrol 2031. Boundary dispute: Jack SSN-605 as separate class. Initial validation finding suggested missing class; research verified Jack as Permit-class member with experimental contra-rotating propellers, not separate class. Decision: included in Thresher/Permit class roster. Boundary dispute: Tullibee SSN-597 as separate class vs. variant. Single-ship experimental design; decision: included as distinct class because commissioned with unique propulsion system (turbo-electric drive) and configuration (bow sonar, amidships torpedo tubes).

research_summary.paragraph: USS Plunger (SS-2) was an Adder Class submarine torpedo boat laid down on 21 May 1901 at Crescent Shipyard, Elizabethport, N.J. She was launched on 1 February 1902 and commissioned on 19 September 1903. On 25 August 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt dove aboard the vessel off Long Island Sound, spending three hours underwater. The submarine was renamed USS A-1 on 17 November 1911 and was struck from the Naval Register on 24 February 1913. After being designated Target E on 29 August 1916, she was sold for scrapping on 26 January 1922.

She displaced 2000 tons surfaced and 2,506 tons submerged, with a length of 341'6", beam of 27'1", and draft of 14'7". Her armament consisted of 1 5"/51 gun, 4 bow and 2 stern torpedo tubes, and 12 21" torpedoes. She carried a complement of 80 crew members.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Gato (SS-212) was the lead ship of the Gato-class submarines. Named after a species of small catshark found in waters along the west coast of Mexico, her keel was laid on 5 October 1940 and she was launched on 21 August 1941. Gato was commissioned on 31 December 1941 and decommissioned on 16 March 1946. She later served as a Naval Reserve Training vessel before being placed out of service and struck from the Naval Register on 1 March 1960. Gato was sold for scrap on 25 July 1960.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Balao (SS-285) was a Balao-class submarine built at Portsmouth Navy Yard in Kittery, Maine. Her keel was laid on 26 June 1942, she was launched on 27 October 1942, and she was commissioned on 4 February 1943. The submarine displaced 1,526 tons surfaced and 2,424 tons submerged, measured 311 feet in length, and could reach 20 knots surfaced and 9 knots submerged. Armament included 6 bow and 4 stern torpedo tubes with 24 torpedoes. She carried a crew complement of 80. USS Balao was decommissioned on 20 August 1946.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Tench (SS-417) was the lead ship of the Tench-class submarines. Built at Portsmouth Navy Yard, her keel was laid on 1 April 1944, she was launched on 7 July 1944, and commissioned on 6 October 1944. The submarine displaced 1,570 tons surfaced and 2,414 tons submerged, measured 311'8" in length, and was armed with 6 bow and 4 stern torpedo tubes carrying 24 torpedoes. She was reclassified as AGSS-417 on October 1, 1969, decommissioned on May 8, 1970, and struck from the Naval Register on August 16, 1973.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Tang (SS-563) was the second ship to bear the name Tang. Her keel was laid on 18 April 1949 at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, she was launched on 19 June 1951, and commissioned on 25 October 1951. The new Tang introduced the fast attack concept to the submarine community with its streamlined hull, integrated snorkel system, and increased speed and depth. She was described as the first of the modern fast attack submarines and surrogate parent of the U.S. Navy's nuclear power submarine force. In 1980, USS Tang was decommissioned as the oldest diesel-electric submarine in the Navy and the last operational one in the Atlantic Fleet.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Albacore (AGSS-569) was an experimental submarine that represented a radical change in submarine design. Designed, built, and maintained by Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, Albacore was launched on August 1st, 1953 and served as a research submarine until 1972. The hull was designed with underwater speed as the prime requirement, and it was built with newly developed high-strength steel (HY-80). The vessel pioneered the teardrop-shaped hull and featured a true underwater hull of cylindrical shape that has become the standard for today's submarines worldwide.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Barbel (SS-580) was a Barbel-class submarine built at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Her keel was laid on 18 May 1956, she was launched on 19 July 1958, and commissioned on 17 January 1959. The submarine was decommissioned on 4 December 1989 and struck from the Naval Register on 17 January 1990. USS Barbel was ultimately sunk as a target on 30 January 2001.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Skipjack (SSN-585) was a Skipjack-class nuclear attack submarine built by General Dynamics Electric Boat Division in Groton, Connecticut. Her keel was laid on 29 May 1956, she was launched on 26 May 1958, and commissioned on 15 April 1959. The submarine had a surface displacement of 3,075 tons and a submerged displacement of 3,513 tons. She was decommissioned on 19 April 1990 and struck from the Naval Register the same day. The vessel was disposed of through the Nuclear-Powered Ship and Submarine Recycling Program on 17 March 1996.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Thresher (SSN-593) was a nuclear-powered attack submarine and the lead ship of a new class of fast-attack submarine. Her keel was laid down at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, ME in 1958. The submarine was the culmination of twelve years of scientific and engineering research to develop a submarine hunter-killer to address the threat that Soviet submarines posed. USS Thresher was lost on April 10, and a search was subsequently conducted for the vessel.

research_summary.paragraph: USS Seawolf (SSN-21) is a Seawolf-class attack submarine and the fourth U.S. Navy submarine to bear the name Seawolf. Her keel was laid on 25 October 1989, she was launched and christened on 24 June 1995, and she was commissioned on 19 July 1997.

research_summary.paragraph: SSBN-598 USS George Washington was the world's first nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine. The designation SSBN means Ship Submersible Ballistic (Nuclear), with "Nuclear" referring to the ship's propulsive power. On 15 November 1960, USS George Washington deployed on its first strategic patrol carrying 16 Polaris A1 missiles. The submarine returned from patrol on 21 January 1961, coming alongside the tender USS Proteus at New London, Connecticut. In the early 1980s, SSBN-598 George Washington had its missiles removed and was reclassified as an attack submarine, a role in which it served for several years prior to decommissioning.

research_summary.paragraph: SSBN-616 USS Lafayette was a Lafayette Class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine built at the Electric Boat Division of General Dynamics in Groton, Connecticut. Her keel was laid on 17 January 1961, and she was launched on 8 May 1962 with First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy serving as sponsor. The submarine was commissioned on 23 April 1963. She served as a Polaris missile submarine during the Cold War. USS Lafayette was decommissioned and struck from the Naval Register on 12 August 1991, with recycling completed on 25 February 1992 at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard.

evidence.quote: John Philip Holland Submarine design, 1870s–1900s Irish immigrant John Philip Holland designed and constructed the U.S. Navy’s first submarine, USS Holland (SS 1). John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at Holland ’s more successful design. Holland included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system. After two years of Navy trials and modifications to Holland, the Navy purchased the submarine on April 11, 1900, for $165,000 (about $4.7 million today). It also ordered seven more Holland -type boats, sufficiently impressed by Holland ’s potential. On October 12, 1900, the U.S. Navy commissioned USS Holland as its first submarine, establishing the U.S. Submarine Force. USS Holland spent most of her ten years in service at the U.S. Naval Academy as a training submarine. The seven new Holland- type submarines, built with Navy-specified improvements, became the Navy’s A -class of submarines.

evidence.quote: John Philip Holland Submarine design, 1870s–1900s Irish immigrant John Philip Holland designed and constructed the U.S. Navy’s first submarine, USS Holland (SS 1). John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at Holland ’s more successful design. Holland included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system. After two years of Navy trials and modifications to Holland, the Navy purchased the submarine on April 11, 1900, for $165,000 (about $4.7 million today). It also ordered seven more Holland -type boats, sufficiently impressed by Holland ’s potential. On October 12, 1900, the U.S. Navy commissioned USS Holland as its first submarine, establishing the U.S. Submarine Force. USS Holland spent most of her ten years in service at the U.S. Naval Academy as a training submarine. The seven new Holland- type submarines, built with Navy-specified improvements, became the Navy’s A -class of submarines.
evidence.locator: DVSU4-E1; R2-E1; source=https://navalunderseamuseum.org/undersea-pioneers2/

SS2.paragraph: USS Plunger (SS-2) was an Adder Class submarine laid down on 21 May 1901 and launched on 1 February 1902. She was commissioned on 19 September 1903. On 25 August 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt dove aboard the vessel. The submarine was renamed USS A-1 on 17 November 1911 and was designated Target E on 29 August 1916. She was sold for scrapping on 26 January 1922.

operator_decision_points.reason: NHHC and most authoritative sources treat Lafayette as single class with subgroups; James Madison and Benjamin Franklin are often called 'subclasses' but share same basic design with minor improvements. To avoid roster padding with near-identical variants, combined under Lafayette class. All 31 boats are Lafayette-class.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Lafayette-class subgroups (James Madison SSBN-627 to 636, Benjamin Franklin SSBN-640 to 645) be listed as separate classes or combined under Lafayette?

operator_decision_points.reason: Four Ohio-class SSBNs (726, 727, 728, 729) converted to SSGNs 2002-2008; conversion of existing class, not new construction. Noted within Ohio class entry. Follows DvsU guidance not to pad roster with mission-kit variants of already-included machines.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Ohio SSGN conversions be listed as a separate class from Ohio SSBN?

operator_decision_points.reason: Title says 'Ever Built' but validation findings clarify scope violation: Columbia (SSBN-826) is under construction (65% complete as of Feb 2026) but not commissioned. An 'ever built' list for submarines means commissioned submarines. Delivery expected 2028, first patrol 2031. Excluded to match title scope.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Columbia class be included when first boat is under construction but not commissioned as of 2026?

operator_decision_points.reason: Title implies 'US submarine class' meaning USN commissioned classes. Turtle was Revolutionary War era (1775) before USN establishment (1794). Intelligent Whale was tested 1866-1872 but never commissioned. Holland (1900) was first commissioned USN submarine. Pre-commissioning experimental craft excluded.
operator_decision_points.question: Should pre-Holland experimental submarines (Turtle, Intelligent Whale) be included?

operator_decision_points.reason: DSRVs are submersible vehicles transported by and operated from mother submarines, not independent submarine classes. They lack independent long-range capability and are not commissioned as submarines. Excluded as vehicles, not submarines.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicles (DSRV-1, DSRV-2) be included?

operator_decision_points.reason: Single-ship experimental nuclear attack submarine class with distinct design. Commissioned 9 November 1960. Tested turbo-electric drive, bow-mounted spherical sonar, amidships torpedo tubes. Fits 'built prototype' bucket and meets inclusion threshold as commissioned submarine. Validation finding confirmed omission.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Tullibee (SSN-597) be included as a separate class?

operator_decision_points.reason: USS Jack (SSN-605) verified as Permit-class member with experimental contra-rotating propellers, not separate class. Wikipedia, NavSource, and multiple sources classify as 'Permit-class submarine' or 'Thresher-class' (same class, renamed). Commissioned 31 March 1967. Included in Thresher/Permit class roster entry.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Jack (SSN-605) be included as a separate class?

operator_decision_points.reason: Validation findings confirmed both as missing commissioned submarine classes. B-class: 3 submarines (SS-10/11/12) commissioned 1907, last Holland-designed submarines. C-class: 5 submarines (SS-9, SS-13-16) commissioned 1908-1910, first two-shaft USN submarines. Both verified through Wikipedia, GlobalSecurity, NavSource, NHHC DANFS.
operator_decision_points.question: Should B-class and C-class be added as separate entries?

operator_decision_points.reason: Validation findings confirmed T-1 class as missing commissioned submarine class. 2 submarines (SST-1/Mackerel, SST-2/Marlin) commissioned 1953. Distinct from Barracuda SSK class. Verified through Wikipedia and NHHC DANFS.
operator_decision_points.question: Should T-1 class training submarines be added as separate entry?

operator_decision_points.reason: Validation findings confirmed correction needed. Barracuda class consisted of 3 hunter-killer submarines (SSK-1/Barracuda, SSK-2/Bass, SSK-3/Bonita) commissioned 1951-1952. Only SSK-1 redesignated SST-3 in 1959. Initial roster conflated this with T-1 class. Corrected entry now shows all 3 submarines.
operator_decision_points.question: Should Barracuda SSK class be corrected to show all 3 submarines?

payload.headline: Every US Submarine Class Ever Built (2026)
payload.fact_sheet: ROSTER DISCOVERY PASS - Full enrichment deferred. Classes verified: Holland SS-1 (1 boat, 1900) through Virginia SSN-799 (26 boats commissioned through April 2026). Total classes: 58 distinct submarine classes including early development (Holland through S-class), V-boats, WWII production (Gato/Balao/Tench), post-WWII diesel (Tang/Barbel), nuclear attack (Nautilus through Virginia), ballistic missile (George Washington through Ohio), experimental (X-1, Albacore, Tullibee, NR-1), training (T-1 class), hunter-killer (Barracuda SSK), and special-purpose types (radar picket, cruise missile). Validation corrections applied: B-class (3 boats, 1907), C-class corrected to 5 boats (SS-9, SS-13-16, 1908-1910), Tullibee SSN-597 (1 boat, 1960), T-1 class (2 boats, 1953), Barracuda SSK class corrected to 3 boats (SSK-1/2/3, 1951-1952). Jack SSN-605 confirmed as Permit-class member. Columbia SSBN-826 excluded as under construction, not commissioned. Sources: Naval History and Heritage Command (primary), Wikipedia, NavSource, GlobalSecurity, Naval News 2026, The Defense Post 2026, USNI News 2026.

independent_coverage_audit.summary: AUDIT FAILED. The roster contains a fundamental classification error that violates the 'every class ever built' scope: it splits the single Plunger class (7 submarines, SS-2 through SS-8, all commissioned 1903) into two separate classes - 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats, though roster lists only 5 member units when there should be 6 remaining boats). NHHC and GlobalSecurity definitively confirm these are one class of 7 submarines, later redesignated A-1 through A-7. The roster's stated boundary claims 'all commissioned USN submarine classes' but artificially inflates the count by splitting a single class. Additionally, the AA-1/T-class situation requires clarification: the WWI-era AA-1 class (3 submarines, SS-52/60/61, commissioned 1920-1922) was renamed T-class, but the roster lists 'T-1 class' as 1953 training submarines, suggesting either a missing WWI class or misidentification of a post-WWII program. The scope_conforms=false because the roster's own classification contradicts authoritative naval records on what constitutes distinct classes.

findings.problem: These are the SAME class. NHHC and multiple authoritative sources confirm the Plunger class comprised 7 submarines (SS-2 through SS-8): Plunger, Adder, Moccasin, Porpoise, Shark, Grampus, and Pike. The roster incorrectly splits this single 7-boat class into 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats), inflating the class count. The class is sometimes called 'Adder class' because USS Adder was first completed, but it is one class, not two.

The roster appears to confuse the WWI-era T-class (AA-1 class) with a different post-WWII designation or has misidentified a training submarine program.

**Act 1:** We meet a naval history student in the Naval History and Heritage Command archive in Washington, D.C., running her fingers along a yellowed photograph of USS Holland, the first submarine ever commissioned in 1900. She's searching for proof that something impossible once worked. The moment she finds the original commissioning document, she gasps—it's real, it's here, it's been real for 126 years. *Micro-insight: "Every revolution starts with someone refusing to believe it can't be done."*

**Act 2:** On a Virginia-class attack submarine berthed in Norfolk, a sonar technician sits in the darkened control room, headphones on, listening to the ocean. His hands move across the console with muscle memory earned over decades as he tracks contacts no one else can hear. He's one of thousands of operators who've kept this invisible fleet running since Nautilus split the atom underwater in 1954. *Micro-insight: "The best weapon is the one your enemy never sees."*

**Act 3:** In the Pentagon's submarine strategy office, a rear admiral stands before a wall of 58 submarine class designations—the full genealogy from Holland through Virginia. She traces the evolution with a laser pointer: each class a response to a threat, each design a calculated gamble. The Virginia-class

Decision: included in Thresher/Permit class roster. Boundary dispute: Tullibee SSN-597 as separate class vs. variant. independent_coverage_audit.summary: AUDIT FAILED. The roster contains a fundamental classification error that violates the 'every class ever built' scope: it splits the single Plunger class (7 submarines, SS-2 through SS-8, all commissioned 1903) into two separate classes - 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats, though roster lists only 5 member units when there should be 6 remaining boats). NHHC and GlobalSecurity definitively confirm these are one class of 7 submarines, later redesignated A-1 through A-7. The roster's stated boundary claims 'all commissioned USN submarine classes' but artificially inflates the count by splitting a single class. Additionally, the AA-1/T-class situation requires clarification: the WWI-era AA-1 class (3 submarines, SS-52/60/61, commissioned 1920-1922) was renamed T-class, but the roster lists 'T-1 class' as 1953 training submarines, suggesting either a missing WWI class or misidentification of a post-WWII program. The scope_conforms=false because the roster's own classification contradicts authoritative naval records on what constitutes distinct classes.

findings.problem: These are the SAME class. NHHC and multiple authoritative sources confirm the Plunger class comprised 7 submarines (SS-2 through SS-8): Plunger, Adder, Moccasin, Porpoise, Shark, Grampus, and Pike. The roster incorrectly splits this single 7-boat class into 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats), inflating the class count. The class is sometimes called 'Adder class' because USS Adder was first completed, but it is one class, not two.
findings.candidate: Plunger class (SS-2) and Adder class (SS-3 through SS-8) listed as separate classes
findings.required_action: Merge entries into single 'Plunger class' (also known as A-class or Adder class) with all 7 submarines (SS-2 through SS-8) as member units

findings.problem: The roster lists 'T-1 class' (SST-1, SST-2) as a 1953 training submarine class, but authoritative sources confirm the AA-1 class (SS-52, SS-60, SS-61) was renamed T-class in 1920. These are WWI-era fleet submarines commissioned 1920-1922, not 1953 training submarines. The roster appears to confuse the WWI-era T-class (AA-1 class) with a different post-WWII designation or has misidentified a training submarine program.
findings.required_action: Verify whether AA-1/T-class (SS-52, SS-60, SS-61, commissioned 1920-1922) is missing from roster, and clarify identity of 'T-1 class' training submarines allegedly commissioned 1953

Excludes pre-USN experimental craft, foreign-built submarines operated by USN, Confederate submarines, conversions/modernizations of existing classes (Guppy, Fleet Snorkel), submersible vehicles (DSRVs), pure paper studies never built, and submarines not yet laid down or commissioned as of 2026.

candidate_excerpts.text: Although often his contributions are often overshadowed by John Holland’s accomplishments, Simon Lake developed several key technologies important to the successful operation of a submarine, including even-keel hydroplanes, ballast tanks, and periscopes. Lake dreamed of building submarines as a child in the 1870s after reading Jules Verne’s Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. In 1894, Lake unveiled his first submarine, Argonaut Junior, a prototype which demonstrated his understanding of diving principles despite its crude construction.

independent_coverage_audit.summary: AUDIT FAILED. The roster contains a fundamental classification error that violates the 'every class ever built' scope: it splits the single Plunger class (7 submarines, SS-2 through SS-8, all commissioned 1903) into two separate classes - 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats, though roster lists only 5 member units when there should be 6 remaining boats). NHHC and GlobalSecurity definitively confirm these are one class of 7 submarines, later redesignated A-1 through A-7. The roster's stated boundary claims 'all commissioned USN submarine classes' but artificially inflates the count by splitting a single class. Additionally, the AA-1/T-class situation requires clarification: the WWI-era AA-1 class (3 submarines, SS-52/60/61, commissioned 1920-1922) was renamed T-class, but the roster lists 'T-1 class' as 1953 training submarines, suggesting either a missing WWI class or misidentification of a post-WWII program. The scope_conforms=false because the roster's own classification contradicts authoritative naval records on what constitutes distinct classes.

findings.problem: These are the SAME class. NHHC and multiple authoritative sources confirm the Plunger class comprised 7 submarines (SS-2 through SS-8): Plunger, Adder, Moccasin, Porpoise, Shark, Grampus, and Pike. The roster incorrectly splits this single 7-boat class into 'Plunger class' (1 boat) and 'Adder class' (5 boats), inflating the class count. The class is sometimes called 'Adder class' because USS Adder was first completed, but it is one class, not two.
findings.candidate: Plunger class (SS-2) and Adder class (SS-3 through SS-8) listed as separate classes
findings.required_action: Merge entries into single 'Plunger class' (also known as A-class or Adder class) with all 7 submarines (SS-2 through SS-8) as member units

findings.problem: The roster lists 'T-1 class' (SST-1, SST-2) as a 1953 training submarine class, but authoritative sources confirm the AA-1 class (SS-52, SS-60, SS-61) was renamed T-class in 1920. These are WWI-era fleet submarines commissioned 1920-1922, not 1953 training submarines. The roster appears to confuse the WWI-era T-class (AA-1 class) with a different post-WWII designation or has misidentified a training submarine program.
findings.required_action: Verify whether AA-1/T-class (SS-52, SS-60, SS-61, commissioned 1920-1922) is missing from roster, and clarify identity of 'T-1 class' training submarines allegedly commissioned 1953

evidence.quote: John Philip Holland Submarine design, 1870s–1900s Irish immigrant John Philip Holland designed and constructed the U.S. Navy’s first submarine, USS Holland (SS 1). John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at Holland ’s more successful design. Holland included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system. After two years of Navy trials and modifications to Holland, the Navy purchased the submarine on April 11, 1900, for $165,000 (about $4.7 million today). It also ordered seven more Holland -type boats, sufficiently impressed by Holland ’s potential. On October 12, 1900, the U.S. Navy commissioned USS Holland as its first submarine, establishing the U.S. Submarine Force. USS Holland spent most of her ten years in service at the U.S. Naval Academy as a training submarine. The seven new Holland- type submarines, built with Navy-specified improvements, became the Navy’s A -class of submarines.

candidate_excerpts.text: John Philip Holland Father of today’s Submarines - 1898 “John Philip Holland (born February 24?, 1841, Liscannor, County Clare, Ireland—died August 12, 1914, Newark, New Jersey, U.S.) was an Irish-born inventor who was the father of the modern submarine. He designed and built the first underwater vessel accepted by the U.S. Navy.” See page for author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons John Philip Holland Father of today’s Submarines - 1898 “John Philip Holland (born February 24?, 1841, Liscannor, County Clare, Ireland—died August 12, 1914, Newark, New Jersey, U.S.) was an Irish-born inventor who was the father of the modern submarine. He designed and built the first underwater vessel accepted by the U.S. Navy.” Following his work in the early 1890s, the design that John Holland presented to the US Navy in 1898 has formed the basis of the designs for all submarines built since. These features include: “Efficient hydrodynamic hull shape [teardrop-shape with bulbous bow and tapered stern] with good seakeeping ability on the open ocean. Separate main and auxiliary ballast systems enable rapid diving and surfacing with minimial changes to the longitudinal center of gravity while underway. Accomplished by operating with full or nearly full ballast tanks when submerged. Allowed precise control of trim angle while submerged. Able to dive to and accurately maintain a significant depth [up of 75 feet (23 m)]. Diving planes provide the means to precisely control depth [stern planes only, located behind the propeller]. Dual propulsion systems driving a single propeller at the stern. Internal combustion engine provides reliable power on the surface, enabling long transits while charging the batteries [up to 200 nautical miles (370 km) at 6 knots] Lead-acid storage batteries provide power to run submerged for a considerable distance [about 30 nautical miles (56 km) at 5.5 knots]. Conning tower for directing ship and weapons activities on the surface or semi-submerged. No periscope. View ports around the top of the conning tower provided the commander with intermittent views while “porpoising” semi-submerged near the surface. Offensive weapons systems. One reloadable torpedo tube at the bow, with three self-propelled torpedoes carried internally. One pneumatic dynamite gun at the bow that, on the surface, fired large projectiles, sometimes called “aerial torpedoes.” [This was subsequently removed]. John P. Holland first demonstrated the Holland VI to the U.S. Navy on 17 March 1898.” 18 https://lynceans.org/all-posts/a-brief-look-back-at-the-worlds-first-modern-submarine-2/ USS Holland (SS-1) internal and external arrangements. The interior space was one contiguous compartment.
